text: National Weather Service Birmingham’s event page documents the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado of April 27, 2011 in central Alabama. It identifies the tornado as an EF3 event affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, with an estimated maximum wind speed of 145 mph, a path length of 72.13 miles, and a maximum width of 1 mile. The page describes NWS meteorologists’ ground surveys and characterizes the event as a strong tornado. It provides start and end coordinates and times, overall casualty figures (50 injuries and 7 fatalities), and detailed narrative damage descriptions by county. The narrative explains how intensity evolved along the path: starting as EF1 in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River, strengthening to EF2 within Greene County, intensifying to EF3 just north of Sawyerville in Hale County and again around Eoline in Bibb County, and then weakening to EF2 south of West Blocton before dissipating northeast of Marvel. It outlines specific locations crossed (various county roads and state highways), structures destroyed (numerous mobile homes, single-family homes, churches, the Eoline Fire Department, and another business), and widespread tree damage, and notes that tornado warnings were in effect for all three counties during the event.

The report compares this outbreak’s severity and death toll with past large outbreaks such as the 1974 Super Outbreak and the 1965 Palm Sunday Outbreak, noting that April 2011 produced comparable or higher fatality totals. title: Lead
content: The 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a long-track, strong tornado that occurred on April 27, 2011 in central Alabama, United States, during the multi-day April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak often referred to as the April 2011 Super Outbreak. The tornado tracked from far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River west of Tishabee around 5:30 pm Central Daylight Time (CDT) to an area just northeast of Marvel in northeastern Bibb County around 6:55 pm, following a generally northeastward path through Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties. The National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Forecast Office in Birmingham officially rated the tornado EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with an estimated maximum wind speed of about 145 mph (233 km/h), and characterized it as a strong tornado. title: Impacts and casualties
content:

The tornado destroyed the Eoline Fire Department building and another business, and caused major tree damage in the Talladega National Forest and adjacent areas. In Hale County, the NWS documentation reports at least forty injuries and six fatalities associated with extensive structural damage in the Sawyerville–Havana area, with fatality details in the Storm Events Database indicating that deaths occurred largely in mobile homes and similar structures. A later summary on Tornado Talk cites a slightly higher total of fifty-two injuries for the tornado while retaining the figure of seven fatalities, illustrating minor differences between secondary accounts and the primary NWS data. [1][8][9]

title: Aftermath and legacy
content:
The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred on the same day as several higher-profile tornadoes in Alabama, including violent long-track events that affected larger population centers, and subsequent news retrospectives have noted that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado received comparatively less public attention despite its severity. Coverage by outlets such as CBS 42 has placed the Sawyerville–Eoline EF3 tornado within a list of significant April 27, 2011 tornadoes in Alabama, while also emphasizing that the broader outbreak produced numerous violent and long-track tornadoes across the state. Tornado Talk describes the tornado as intense and long-track, notes that it was overshadowed by other concurrent events, and highlights its substantial impacts on small communities and rural areas along the Sawyerville–Eoline corridor. [9][11]

Local and regional accounts reflecting on the April 27, 2011 outbreak have included recollections from emergency management personnel and residents in Hale County, where the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado caused concentrated damage and casualties. These retrospective narratives emphasize the challenges of responding to a severe tornado in a rural area with dispersed housing, mobile homes, and limited infrastructure, within the context of a day that involved multiple simultaneous tornado emergencies. [6][12]
